title: Rutherford I — Viable
disclaimer: For professional education and simulation only. Not for direct patient-care decision-making.
synthetic_findings: Sudden unilateral lower-limb pain and coolness
Limb viable and not immediately threatened

stages.title: Stage 1: Initial recognition and focused assessment
stages.narrative: A synthetic patient develops sudden unilateral lower-limb pain and coolness. Sensation and motor function are intact, and arterial and venous Doppler signals remain audible.
stages.question: What is the best initial educational response to this presentation?
stages.rationale: Acute limb ischemia remains possible despite preserved neurological function and audible Doppler signals. Urgent focused assessment should establish symptom timing, perfusion, motor and sensory status, and possible causes.
stages.safety_principle: A viable limb is not immediately threatened, but preserved sensation and strength must not create false reassurance or routine discharge.

choices.text: Recognize possible acute limb ischemia and perform an urgent focused vascular and neurological assessment
choices.feedback: This identifies the time-sensitive arterial presentation while confirming that the limb remains viable.

choices.text: Consider the limb safe because sensation and strength are preserved and arrange routine follow-up
choices.feedback: Preserved neurological function supports viability but does not exclude acute limb ischemia or remove the need for urgent evaluation.

choices.text: Defer the bedside viability assessment until formal anatomical imaging is available
choices.feedback: Bedside vascular and neurological assessment establishes urgency and should not be postponed for imaging.

choices.text: Restrict the assessment to venous thrombosis because arterial Doppler flow is still audible
choices.feedback: An audible arterial signal does not exclude a partial or distal arterial occlusion, so an arterial assessment remains necessary.

stages.title: Stage 2: Rutherford classification
stages.narrative: The synthetic limb has no sensory loss, no motor weakness, an audible arterial Doppler signal, and an audible venous Doppler signal.
stages.question: Which Rutherford category best matches these findings?
stages.rationale: A limb without sensory or motor deficit and with audible arterial and venous Doppler signals is viable, Rutherford I, and is not immediately threatened.
stages.safety_principle: Rutherford classification is dynamic; any new sensory or motor deficit requires immediate reassessment and escalation.

choices.text: Rutherford I — Viable
choices.feedback: The preserved neurological examination and audible Doppler signals support a viable Rutherford I limb.

choices.text: Rutherford IIa — Marginally threatened
choices.feedback: Rutherford IIa usually includes at least minimal sensory loss, which is absent in this synthetic case.

choices.text: Rutherford IIb — Immediately threatened
choices.feedback: An immediately threatened limb has a more extensive sensory deficit and motor weakness, neither of which is present.

choices.text: Rutherford III — Irreversible
choices.feedback: Irreversible ischemia requires profound anesthesia and paralysis with absent arterial and venous Doppler signals.

stages.title: Stage 3: Immediate management
stages.narrative: The synthetic limb remains viable. No contraindication to anticoagulation has been identified, but the cause and arterial anatomy are not yet defined.
stages.question: Which immediate management approach is most appropriate for the case conference?
stages.rationale: A viable acute ischemic limb still requires urgent vascular-surgery assessment, intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, analgesia and supportive care, and repeated vascular and neurological reassessment.
stages.safety_principle: Viability allows orderly urgent evaluation, not routine discharge or delay; anticoagulation contraindications and progression must remain under review.

choices.text: Arrange urgent vascular-surgery review, give intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, provide supportive care, and repeat limb assessments
choices.feedback: This addresses thrombus propagation, comfort, specialist evaluation, and surveillance for deterioration.

choices.text: Wait for all anatomical and etiological imaging before considering anticoagulation or specialist review
choices.feedback: Routine delay may permit propagation or progression; imaging completion alone is not a reason to defer the urgent pathway.

choices.text: Use outpatient antiplatelet therapy alone because arterial and venous Doppler signals are audible
choices.feedback: Audible signals support viability but do not make an acute arterial presentation suitable for routine outpatient management.

choices.text: Begin anticoagulation but postpone vascular-surgery assessment unless a neurological deficit develops
choices.feedback: Anticoagulation does not replace urgent specialist assessment, anatomical definition, and etiological planning.

stages.title: Stage 4: Diagnostic imaging and treatment planning
stages.narrative: The synthetic limb remains Rutherford I after initial management, providing time for prompt anatomical and etiological evaluation without neglecting reassessment.
stages.question: What is the best diagnostic and planning approach?
stages.rationale: Prompt anatomical imaging should define the occlusion and guide treatment, while evaluation considers embolic, thrombotic, graft-related, aneurysmal, traumatic, and other causes.
stages.safety_principle: Diagnostic evaluation should remain urgent and must be accelerated if sensory loss, weakness, or Doppler deterioration appears.

choices.text: Obtain prompt anatomical imaging and investigate the likely embolic, thrombotic, graft-related, aneurysmal, traumatic, or other etiology
choices.feedback: This uses the viable interval to define anatomy and cause while preserving an urgent treatment pathway.

choices.text: Avoid anatomical imaging because an audible arterial Doppler signal excludes a clinically important occlusion
choices.feedback: An audible signal does not exclude a partial, distal, or collateralized acute occlusion.

choices.text: Define the arterial anatomy but omit etiological assessment because cause does not influence future management
choices.feedback: Etiology affects treatment selection and prevention of recurrence, so it remains a core part of planning.

choices.text: Discharge the patient and arrange elective vascular imaging only if symptoms remain after several days
choices.feedback: A viable acute ischemic limb still requires prompt specialist-led anatomical evaluation.

stages.title: Stage 5: Definitive management and escalation
stages.narrative: Imaging confirms an acute arterial lesion. The limb remains neurologically intact and viable while anatomy and etiology are reviewed.
stages.question: Which definitive-management principle is most appropriate?
stages.rationale: Rutherford I allows appropriate anatomical and etiological evaluation, but treatment remains urgent and individualized to anatomy, etiology, symptom duration, comorbidity, bleeding risk, and local expertise.
stages.safety_principle: Continued viability does not justify neglect; new sensory loss or weakness changes the limb-threat category and accelerates the pathway.

choices.text: Choose an urgent individualized medical, endovascular, surgical, or hybrid plan based on anatomy, cause, duration, comorbidity, bleeding risk, and expertise
choices.feedback: This uses the viable interval for informed planning without converting acute limb ischemia into routine follow-up.

choices.text: Use catheter-directed thrombolysis for every viable acute limb regardless of anatomy, cause, or bleeding risk
choices.feedback: No single technique is appropriate for every anatomy, etiology, and risk profile.

choices.text: Provide reassurance and routine follow-up because the limb is not immediately threatened
choices.feedback: Rutherford I is viable but still represents acute limb ischemia requiring urgent specialist-led management.

choices.text: Treat primary amputation as the default strategy for a neurologically intact viable limb
choices.feedback: A Rutherford I limb is viable and does not support primary amputation as the routine educational direction.
